So I had this on my wishlist for awhile, and picked it up with the soundtrack and DLC on a bundle deal for $20.  While the game looks pretty and the gunplay feels ok, the swapping from third person to first person in the middle of fast paced combat in small areas was extremely jarring to me.  I will say however, it's not bad for what it is. 

At this point in gaming, I'd rather support a small project like this; delivering a completed project, than what AAA games are doing with the predatory monetization and releasing parts of games to milk us for more money in content grabs and cash shops.

[h1]In-Depth[/h1]
[h3]Writing & Worldbuilding[/h3]
In the near-future 2030, Shelia Tan works as an operative for the SRO, a paranormal research organization tasked with keeping in check all things otherworldly that may threaten humanity. Without much introduction to the lore or situation at hand, the cute anime girl / killing machine is summoned by her superiors to investigate a… *checks notes* [i]black hole[/i] that randomly spawned outside the city’s boundaries.

This -completely plausible- incipit starts the short story of BMI, which is as barebones as it gets. The few named characters, be them bosses or otherwise, or even Sheila herself, barely have any screen time and don’t explain their motives, reasoning or plans at all. It’s as ‘B-Movie’ as it gets, with the plot completely annihilated in favor of raw, unadulterated action; this may even be a good choice considering the total runtime. 

The locations and environments are mostly inspired by rural China; in the same way, some enemies are as well, in the mythological aspect. Each area is rich in detail, delivering graphics you could expect from top-tier AAA titles, with great optimization on top of that. Despite the amazing looks, no location really feels iconic or distinct, but instead they feel generic, serving as little more than containers for the enemies and bosses. 

[h3]Exploration & Secrets[/h3]
Each stage is linear, with regular one-way drops and transitions that prevent backtracking, which is expected from the genre, after all. Side locations that contain secrets or extra supplies are present, although in a limited amount and just slightly branching out from the main path - don’t expect wholly standalone side areas or optional open areas. Taking extra time to look for skill points, special ammo and the occasional new weapon is definitely worth your time, as only in that way you’ll gain enough skill points to have a varied roster of abilities later on. Don’t worry about getting lost or orientating: the levels are linear and streamlined enough so that this doesn’t become a problem at all.

[h3]Combat System & Bosses[/h3]
The combat system of BMI plays out in a fast-paced way, having you alternate not only four different guns with normal and special fire modes, but also several active skills for your sword and power gauntlet, other than being able to jump, sprint and dodge frequently. Fights are usually against a handful of enemies that however, save for the basic weak grunts, are all to be considered a threat, and have unique movesets and behaviors each. 

You’ll be able to adapt to the playstyle you prefer based on your skill choices, but generally all options are viable: stay at a distance and destroy your enemies with a rain of bullets - which will take longer, but is also the safest way - or go into the fray and use melee, energy push / pull and the parry system to perform high risk, high reward combos that can annihilate enemies quickly. Tougher enemies have shields in addition to normal health, and they need to be destroyed with attacks or parries in order to deal full damage and render them susceptible to control effects like slow, pushback and so on. 

One of the main issues of the combat system is that you can block indefinitely without any stamina or limit to this mechanic - 90% of all attacks can harmlessly bounce off your sword, even if there are some exceptions to the rule, mostly with bosses. Given that HP auto-regens, you can just kite foes around while blocking and regain HP easily. Bosses don’t have evolving phases, but are generally varied enough in movesets to  be interesting to fight, even if some can become quite trivial with the right skills (I’m looking at you, Tian Yu Emperor, getting perma-staggered by blade skills), but still they’re interesting and unique enough. 

[h3]Character Progression[/h3]
You’ll be able to gain skill points by either finding them (Reliquaries) or by collecting blue orbs from the enemies and breakable objects in the environment; ten orbs is one Reliquary, as in one skill point. There’s not enough to unlock all skills, so you’ll have to focus on what you prefer and think is best. From AoE to single target specific skills, the blade and gauntlet powers will enable you to deliver devastating attacks from a distance, with additional effects like damage over time, auto tracking and more.

I'm so conflicted about Bright Memory: Infinite. The gameplay is (mostly) incredible, it's fun as hell, and it looks amazing. But what even is this product? I thought the original Bright Memory was meant to be a tech demo for a full game but this "bigger" release is barely longer than its demo. You can see everything this game has to offer in under two hours and after that you just have different difficulties to play and...skins to unlock? This game feels like it's banking real hard on you caring about dressing up your waifu. The story is also complete nonsense and quite literally goes nowhere. I'd almost rather it not be there at all. As soon as I felt like it was really hitting its stride the game just ends extremely abruptly.

For anyone who bough the original Bright Memory and got this upgrade free, congrats it's a good deal, but for anyone else it's just baffling. Why in this under two-hour game is there a forced stealth section and a bad driving level? Is this actually a game or someone's resume?

I'm just so torn. Bright Memory: Infinite is both rad as hell and a massive missed opportunity as it still feels like a fraction of a larger game.

This is one of those games where you have to look at it from a whole in order to appreciate it. This game's original team consisted entirely of one person. While others could have joined the team later on, that was who came up with the concept. Given that, it's very impressive.

For starters I love the game play. It could stand to allow me to change the button scheme and skip cut scenes, but it's a short enough game (around 2 hours, give or take) that this wasn't a huge deal.

Don't expect much from the story, It's more reminiscent of the original early era Playstation games where there's no real story to it. You're just fighting bad guys because. This also means that character development is non existent. It also means that the game play gets a little silly. Random stealth mission? Sure. Car chase? Why not?

The ending has a very obvious anti American political prod, but okay. It is still worth purchasing and having a lot of fun with.

Actual reviewish thoughts on the game!

I've really enjoyed the first Bright Memory game, even though it was a short and felt almost as some sort of tech demo like experience.

Bright Memory Infinite is a tad longer, with rock solid robust gameplay, gunplay that is fun, with weapons that pack a punch. Furthermore Shelia, the protagonist, additionally wields a sword that can be used to defend urself and makes us of special skills in battle, out of which  two are unlocked and two are unlockable; all four being upgradeable.

The story, as little as is there, is as B movieish as it can be and only serves to rush the player from one crazy action sequence to the next. People have been complaining about unskipable cutscenes and yes that is what they are, but they are very short and imho serve as a short break for the player to catch their breath.

Graphics, yes the Graphics, they are beautiful and make feel proud about ur investment in a RTX card. At leasts that what I think. They are stunning at times indeed.

Conclusion:
Overall, I had a blast with Bright Memory Infinite. Truth be told, it is still pretty much an indie game and it does show, but the robust and fun gameplay, combined with some truly beautiful graphics and fitting nice soundtrack and voiceovers make this one a fun, even though short over the top experience that any action and fps player can and will enjoy!! Furthermore credit must be given to the dev for constantly working on improving their game.

Highly recommend and I hope this developer releases more gameplay someday.

Pros:
-Really enjoyable experience.
-Enjoyable mechanics in terms of your abilities and weapons, as well as movement shooter-esque wallrunning and dashing.
-Nice mix of Ranged and Melee combat.
-Neat mythological atmosphere.
-Shows a lot of promise for what comes next from this studio.

Cons:
-A bit short (About 2 hours of gameplay).
-Story was lacking in many areas. Characters are kinda just there to be there. One of them literally only exists to drop in specific utilities once every mission. Story kinda just boils down to "Oh no, big bag thing happening, gotta save the world now".
-Mechanics, while very enjoyable, are a little unrefined and a bit janky at times. (Wallrunning is a bit short and has a weird arc. You can dash in every direction but forward which is a slide move. Grappling hook is a bit odd in general.)
-Controls for gamepad are not remappable and are a bit weird. This is easily remedied with the Steam Controller config, but nothing beats native control remapping.
-$20 is too high of a price.

Neither Pros nor Cons:
-Seems to have a sort of speedrun aspect to it, because at the end of a playthrough, it gives you a score. This is implemented kinda weirdly to the point where it doesn't really make itself known until you've completed the game. So, if your into speedrun games, this is a pro. If not, it doesn't impact gameplay at all, so no big deal.
-Characters' reactions are kinda underdone. I, for one, found it absolutely hilarious when something absolutely insane happens and the characters just kind of brush it off as if it's a normal thing. Although, this could be seen as a con to some people.

For what it is, I would definitely recommend it to anyone who's looking for a short and fun experience. It's really strong in its gameplay aspects, but lacking in story, length, and character depth.

Bright Memory: Infinite is not a sequel to Bright Memory but sort of a full version of that early tech-demo game we saw years prior. This game came free to anyone who bought the original Bright Memory but to everyone else this game cost $20.

The strongest suit of Bright Memory: Infinite is the amazing visuals and the explosive combat, probably one of the best form of first-person shooter combat. Fast movements and satisfying gunplay on top of being able to swing around your sword gives me a mix feeling of Devil May Cry and Metal Gear: Revengence. This is insanely impressive, given how this game was developed by a single person. WIth the impressive use of ray-tracing, this game give us a glimpse on what future games are capable of.

However, even with the impressive visuals, it is mostly due to the lighting and water effects. Otherwise, the in game models and even environmental textures aren't all that impressive. The game is also a tad buggy in some areas but nothing too game breaking. The biggest sin I encounter is the fact that the game is very inconsistent with performance. In some areas I was able to clock in about 120fps with ray-tracing at the highest setting where in some areas I would struggle to even stay above 30fps while turning down the ray-trace settings.

The story is as nonsensical as it can get making Kingdom Hearts look straight forward so don't expect to go into this game to get a good story or understanding anything. The world is a mix of ancient-chinese, magic, and sci-fi so its cool enough as a presentation but thats about it. Voice acting is... there. Not really great but the protagonist gets a pass at least.

Bright Memory: Infinite is a fun first person shooter that makes you feel like an action movie hero.

The beautiful graphics and fun gameplay stand out as the best parts. Fast paced combat with shooting, dodging, reflecting enemy bullets or even parrying if blocking melee attacks at the right time. It rewards high paced action since the stamina meter regenerates faster if you are moving all the time. Apart from having 4 different weapons with alternative fire modes, Sheila has access to her sword and powerful abilities that can suspend an enemy mid air, burst a lot of damage after charging an attack or combo an enemy by lifting him in the air. Fighting the ranged enemies can feel weird since they shoot at odd intervals so sometimes it looks like they are just watching instead of shooting you while you stand still in front of them. But the melee enemies and boss fights are more fun with fast dodges and parries.

Levels are linear with some invisible walls, but they are filled with a lot of scripted events to keep them dynamic. Some levels are purely cinematic with a few quick time events and some parts of the levels have wall running or using a grapple that has no purpose but to look cool and it delivers on the cool factor. The missions are varied with an obligatory stealth sequence where all your weapons are unusable, car chase, fighting on a plane and an epic boss fight at the end.

The voice acting is well done and the story does it's job to keep the intense action rolling, but beyond that, there's nothing there. While it may be a fun action game, it's short with a length of only 2 hours, so unless you got it for free because of the first game, it might be worth waiting for a sale.

For achievement hunters:
The achievements are for completing the last mission on the harder difficulties and for various weapon, skill or reliquary grinds with a chapter select available.

Bright Memory: Infinite is a short, action packed shooter that offers nothing more than some mindless action. However, it's worth knowing that all of it was made by a single guy so, I'll have to give him credit for creating such a wonderful FPS that resembles Crysis. It feels quite satisfying to dodge and repel bullets, slice enemies in half with your Lightblade, pull them close by using your Exo Unit Arm and blast them to pieces by sending a powerful EMP pulse. The extend of skills that you can use doesn't end there of course. As you progress through the game, you collect certain materials to upgrade and unlock new skills to unleash all kinds of chaos. 

The story is not good and I personally had no idea what was going on with that ending despite getting all achievements which means that I've beaten the game at least 3 times. There's this black hole anomaly that you're supposed to inspect and then there is this Ancient King who tries to change the world by spilling the Primordial Flame? There's also this guy that gets involved in story in the middle of it who's apparently the top dog of the opposing company? Look, all of that stuff doesn't make any sense and it's quite obvious that the story is just there to fill the void. It's only a 2 hours long game anyway. 

Lip sync and animation quality is slightly better in this one but they are nowhere near to be qualified as "good" and apart from the janky animation quality, I personally witnessed only one game breaking bug which was clipping out of the map on my first playthrough but it was easy enough to fix by simply reloading the checkpoint. The bosses can also get glitchy in some circumstances but it doesn't prevent you from progressing further. Speaking of bosses, I can say that the developer did a wonderful job with them since they are quite good. However, the fact that the whole game is kinda distant from the demo really puts me off. I mean, I expected to find collectible relics that are related to story and more enemy variety with a little bit of Tomb Raider vibe going on. Sadly, Infinite is not like that. Demo also made it look like Wake could be another playable character only to be reduced to a helicopter pilot in this one. 

[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
A short action packed FPS that heavily resembles Crysis. It's also made by a single guy so, if you're in it for some mindless action and have zero expectations from the story, Bright Memory: Infinite won't disappoint.
A short, fun and great mix of FPS and hack n slash action made by one person, really impressed just like its previous game, great improvement over it.

Inspired by various famous action and shooter titles, Bright Memory Infinite is the extended version of Bright Memory from 2019, which received lots of praise for being a one-man project with great graphics and the creativity to combine action game mechanics with FPS. Built upon it, Bright Memory Infinite has brand new contents and is much more integrated and refined mechanically. It is a short-lived (three hours on highest difficulty available at the get-go) but very impressive and pleasant experience with fluid and fanatic fast-paced combat.

The way the game integrated action into shooter is by three mechanics: enhanced movement, allowing fast movement and high jumping; EXO device that can freeze, levitate and pull enemy and do powerful punch; light blade which acts as a close and mid-range weapon that can also levitate enemy and more importantly, as a mechanic to block and counter. These mechanics require a bit of practice to master, but it is them that make this game so special compared to other shooters. Combined with the excellent shooting that is on par with 3A shooters, the experience is so delightful and satisfying. However, these mechanics were not made full use of due to the level and enemy design.

Enhanced movement can only be used in dodging and only two short platforming sessions because there is basically no verticality in level design. And much like COD: Advanced Warfare which also has enhanced movement, both games have lots of invisible walls. Sometimes you can jump up to higher places, but invisible walls stop you from using it for combat. For COD, it is because of the least amount of effort to replicate Titanfall and for this game is due to budget, but nevertheless, both fail to utilize it to spice up the combat.

I basically forgot the EXO device and only used it a handful of times for crowd control. The enemy design largely contributes to this, since the elite enemies, who you want to use the device to, have “shields” that can protect them from freezing and being pulled and levitated. You must break the shield first and in the process of doing so, it is more convenient to kill them straight-up. As for the punch, it takes time to charge so you might as well use your blade.

As for the blade, the counter timing is 0.3 sec before the hits, which is very confusing and counterintuitive since people are more used to counter at the exact time when the attack lands. If you counter successfully, your gun will reload automatically so that you can keep attacking. But since you can easily get out of attack zone to reload, the benefit is not that attractive considering the tricky timing and the risk of getting hit. Also, I first thought the shield of the boss needs counter to break, since the game takes inspiration from Devil May Cry where many bosses cannot be attacked straight-up. It could be very interesting but unfortunately, this game doesn’t have it. You can break their shields using whatever attack, making counter far less needed. 

Asides from counter, levitation (for both blade and EXO device) also suffer from enemy design. In Devil May Cry where this game takes this idea from, you are incentivized to levitate enemies because others cannot hit you when you are in mid-air doing combo. Whereas in this game long-range enemies are not well-balanced, their projectiles have no trouble hitting you in mid-air, interrupting your combo and discouraging you from levitating enemies, not to mention you need to go through the hassle of breaking their shields first.

Overall, I think the level and enemy design really crippled the action mechanics, not only fail to add more necessity to make use of them, but also disincentivize players from using them. The combat could have been in the next level if they were more properly designed, but for now, they make the action part, which is the gem of the game, largely underutilized.

Additionally, there are some trivial issues regarding the enemy and level design, shooting and control.
[list]
    [*]Enemy AI often glitches out - just stand there doing nothing unless they are attacked.
    [*]You often get attacked from the back because enemies spawn out of thin air and it is very glaring.
    [*]Sniper has unreasonably short TTD. Not as horrendous as Kig-Yar in Halo 2, still, they take you out in no time (two shots at Revenge Difficulty) if you don’t take care of them as soon as they spawn in.
    [*]Some elite enemies don’t give out obvious attack signals, or it is too brief to react on, making block and counter very uncomfortable.
    [*]The boss design is not as good as Dark Souls or Devil May Cry, but far better than most generic shooters. However, the final boss is unpleasant to fight, with a giant health pool and tons of attacks that cannot be blocked or countered.
    [*]There is a stealth level in this short game, which I suspect simply for the sake of making it longer. It is very out-of-place, as players want more fast-paced combat, not a slow and half-baked stealth session.
    [*]I don’t hate the driving level, but it is not well-designed as you have to turn the car to shoot because the direction of the car cannon is fixed.
    [*]They really should make the shotgun full-auto and reload faster in this fast-paced game.
    [*]Unlike most games where reload is finished as soon as reload animation is done, in this game it is about a second later than animation and the actual indicator is bullet counter turns white from red. As doing any input other than movement will cause the reload unfinished, you often end up halting the reload accidentally with this less noticeable indicator.
    [*]Shooting has a few frustrating bugs: your gun gets auto reload if you keep shooting once the ammo is out, but it glitches out constantly; bullet number is different before and after death and sometimes even changes after swapping guns; switching fire mode often bugs out and cannot be changed, but sometimes the gun changes fire mode itself.
    [*]It doesn’t make any sense to use Tab over Q as the default block button because Tab + Shift is the combination for in-game Steam interface.
    [*]I much appreciate the control scheme as it minimizes the number of used buttons by making use of long/short press and combined keys for different functions. But using F for both pick up and freezing enemy is not a good idea because the hitbox for pick up is very imprecise. The best solution is to implement auto pick up for there is no necessity to have manual pick up in this game.
[/list]
As for graphics, it is a treat. It uses a cold and clean color tone and reflection similar to Crysis 2 and 3 and Battlefield 4 Shanghai level, and also implements traditional Chinese aesthetic in environmental and enemy design, making the game look very beautiful and special. But human faces and motion look stiff and anti-aliasing is not perfect, causing some textures to look off and far objects and underwater to look grainy. Though it has some occasional frame drops, optimization in general is good.

Game Spot accurately summed up the story as “unintelligible”. The developer tried to make an open-ended story, but shot themselves in the foot as the story feels like starting a movie in the middle. The writing is bad, full of nonsense terminologies for world-building that are useless for better storytelling. John Carmack, the lead programmer of Quake once said, “Story in a game is like a story in porn.” This game is the kind of game he talked about. You don’t come for the story anyway.

The game is fairly buggy and needs some updates to iron things out, but the experience is good and still intact. Though I talked about a lot of issues and why the potential is not fully realized, the actual downside is no others but the short length. I hope in the future they can utilize the action elements better with wiser assistive design and make the next game longer.

+ I have to say, and I didn't expect to say this but the level design is quite good!!! There is a stealth mission and it's honestly better than most stealth missions I've recently played in other games. 
+ Needless to say the visuals are veeeeeeery good. Especially with RTX and DLSS turned on. 

- The characters and story and the voice acting are all pretty bad. But hey, if you're here for the visuals and the gameplay, you're in the right place!

Edit - FYI Regarding performance, I have a laptop RTX 3070 135W with i7 11800h. I run the game at 1440p all max settings and DLSS turned on.
At ray tracing set to high, I get 70-100 fps.
At ray tracing set to medium, I get 90-130 fps.
Ultra high is pointless so I didn't try.

I have minor gripes, the fact that you can't use any other form of attack while doing a charge move make them hard to combo with and makes them unnecessarily risky as it makes you almost a sitting duck, but the core combat is generally pretty good.

The problems really start with the level design. First of all, its linear, REALLY linear. This on its own is not a problem, but it becomes one when the game try's to have you look around to find upgrade points. Since the levels don't have enough room to explore for them it usually means the are either in plain sight, or in a small corner in a combat zone. Mindlessly looking through rooms you just cleared is already not fun but it gets worse when you add in all the "realistic" detail and the mostly outdoor setting. Those just make the environments feel even smaller by forcing you to confront the artificial level boundaries often. The lack of real walls in the levels also make wall running not an option in most arenas which feels needlessly limiting. 

The game is also, unfortunately, very short. Now to its credit it does have a good variety of enemy types, especially for such a short game. A good mix of ranged and melee, ancient and futuristic, and humanoid and monster enemies keep thing lively till the end, but that end comes too soon. 

The bosses unfortunately don't share the variety. There are are only three in the and one of the is the same another for its first phase. It really highlights how short the game is that the third boss is the last one.

Now the game does try to encourage replays by ranking you when you beat as well as having multiple difficulty options, but the ranking is vague on what it wants from you and there is no way to track how you are doing mid campaign. This game  really needed to have a DMC type style meter to both track you're ranking progress and encourage varying up what guns and abilities you use.

Now despite the negative rating and most of the text of this review, I actually do like this game. Its just that I see the flaws as well as the potential for this game and cant help but wish for more. I hope FYQD-Studio's next game is better and if you want to buy this one then I actually encourage it. Just be aware of all the flaws.

A remake/reimagining of the original Bright Memory. I reviewed the first a lifetime ago (in 2019. The old and the weak are doomed...) and it was pretty mediocre. However, this is a much better realised game. The goofy pace breaking puzzles from that where you jumped on blocks or whatever are gone, though there's still some issues.

Like the original, this is RAGE 2 meets Shadow Warrior meets Call of Duty Advance Warfare with a light dash of Devil May Cry thrown in. The combat system is pretty fluid and lets you experiment quite a bit without locking you into a specific playstyle: you can shoot, use your sword, throw enemies into the air and juggle them, drag them to you and make them explode, and so on. It's all very good and the hit feedback/enemy reactions/reload animations/etc. for everything related to the combat is appropiately meaty and satisfying and there's collectibles associated to an upgrade system that lets you unlock a few extra moves like a rocket punch.

Unfortunately, while there's no dumb puzzles this time around, there's a forced stealth section a quarter into the game that is a complete bore. Thankfully the enemy AI during it is braindead and at most it shouldn't take longer than 10-20 minutes, but it still sucks. The combat in this game is the star of the show and it reminds me of the new Wolfenstein games where you wonder why they thought it was a good idea since it's not why you are playing the game at all. It should've been straight up removed and only seems to exist to slightly pad out what is a 2 hour game.

The story is also complete nonsense. So nonsensical that I thought it had to be a sequel to the original release and I did more work than anyone should and actually watched a playthrough of that to see if it was and no - like I said before this is a full reimagining/remake. The writing in this is basically tuning into the second season of a TV show with not knowledge of the first with characters already knowing each other and concepts being namedropped without any explanation. Even after two playthroughs none of it made any sense. You are a perfectly coiffed out of place young anime girl in a gritty word and you work for an organization that may or may not investigate dimension hopping/paranomal events. The bad guy also supposedly knows you from previous encounters like a saturday morning cartoon villain and wants a device that will let him rebuild the world or something. There's another bad guy from the Other Dimension who says he'll tell you who he is but nothing ever comes out of that and typing all this is already tiring. It's like playing the follow up to something that doesn't exist.
While the cutscenes are thankfully rare and incredibly brief, there's a really pointless 2 minute intro that you can't skip when starting a new game. Once again, not too bad, but this is a fast paced 2 hour game and that should be skippable (none of the cutscenes in the game are). 

Still, this is a game that remembers that an FPS should be mainly about fun combat with satisfying hit feedback (something that a lot of AAA and indie shooters forget), so for that alone it's easily worth a playthrough or two if you like fast paced shooters.

Bright Memory was an impressive tech demo that was in Steam Early Access a couple of years ago. It had a scantily clad female protagonist (which doesn't do anything for the game honestly) and a mix of sword and gunplay in the first person which felt fast-paced and punchy. Infinite is the fully released game, and it's basically a much longer tech demo. You can finish the game in 90 minutes and this leaves nothing for story or character development which is almost non-existent. All I gathered is that there's a black hole forming near-Earth and you must stop an evil military guy from taking some sort of artifact that will bring Earth back to Feudal Japan? I'm honestly not even sure.

The best part about the game is the gunplay. The swordplay kind of takes a back seat and is only needed in certain situations. You get a standard arsenal of four weapons. Automatic pistol, auto-shotgun, assault rifle, and sniper rifle. Each weapon has an alternate ammo type that's usually explosive and does massive damage which is best saved for larger enemies and bosses. The weapons feel heavy and punchy, and they are fun to shoot and use. The gunplay was so good that it kept me wanting more from the game. It had a AAA budget quality to it that's not seen in many indie shooters. The swordplay consists of mashing a single button or launching enemies into the air. There's a tacked-on afterthought of a skill tree that lets you unlock abilities and upgrade your alternate ammo firepower, but in 90 minutes you upgrade almost everything pretty quickly so it feels trivial.

There is a grapple line for traversing long distances which are scripted, and you can wall run. These ninja acrobatics feels a bit stiff and not as refined as the actual gunplay. In fact, all of the animations feel stiff and like they were hand done. The faces almost don't animate and thankfully there are less than 10 minutes of total screen time where the camera shows any faces. Your main character, Shelia, is questionable in the sexy department since you hardly ever see her and there are DLC costumes that seem pointless due to the short run time. You can go through the game again on higher difficulties, but I don't see the point.

The issue with a short game like this is there is no incentive to come back. There are no modes, no multiplayer, and hardly anything to aim for. The visuals in the game are fantastic with great use of ray-tracing, but again the animations are weird. There's a short scene where you drive a car and it feels really janky and half-baked. Overall, the boss fights are fun, but there are literally only four types of enemies in the whole game so it gets repetitive quickly. At a sale price, this could be a fun evening, but that's about it.

Great game albeit short

From the very start, the atmosphere created with the combination of sound and graphics was excellent. I was instantly impressed.

In just over four hours I've beaten the game twice--first on "Revenge" and then the unlocked "Hell" difficulty, but the core gameplay is fun enough that it makes up for the brevity of play.

Mistakes set you back to reasonable checkpoints, keeping you in the action and avoiding replaying an excess of content just to get back to where you were. To keep up the pace even more, ammunition is generously given to the player and even returned upon death(no retrying a boss with 0 special ammo in this game).

For replayability of difficulties, [strike]there are few cutscenes you can skip for subsequent playthroughs which is annoying--since the game is so short, I get to rewatch cutscenes I saw less than two hours ago.[/strike] More cutscene skips have been added.
The game has a very fun balance between difficulty and fun gameplay--it's not an unfun waste of time to go through Hell mode and you just have to play better (either faster or safer, depending on your style).

The game runs well in comparison to modern fps games: a stable 144 fps on max settings, which is almost unheard of in modern gaming(AAA xd?). For this type of single player title, I didn't feel it necessary to uncap my fps and try to push to 240+fps and it was VERY playable on max difficulty(2080 super 23-25C ambient).

This game also supports NVIDIA Reflex and DLSS which felt great: I had zero input or latency issues, and only two brief instances of fps drops.

The sound design/music are excellent. Absolutely amazing.

Shooting feels good. Abilities feel good. Movement feels good, but it took me a moment to realize how to avoid dodging while trying to sprint since both dodge and sprint are one button. If you only sprint with W, you will never misinput a dodge as there is no forward dodge.

The game allows you to change settings before throwing you into gameplay and story, allowing you to ensure that you don't nearly go deaf and also change some graphics and control options which is an issue in more games than it should be(even in 2021!! ridiculous!).

There are a few issues such as:
Sliding into objects and jumping onto certain things can get you stuck, but I was always able to slide out. [b]edit: A lot of places where you can get stuck have been fixed.[/b]
Enemies can be pushed behind walls, but luckily the walls I did this on were plants and I could shoot the enemies through them.
[strike]There are one or two areas where fps tanks every time I get there, but it recovers within about a minute or so. I did not test this enough to give more clear feedback and instead enjoyed playing the game. The rest of the game is smooth.[/strike] [b]fixed[/b]
Enemies can spawn VERY close to you. Feels a bit weird, but I only suffered one KO from behind.


---The remainder of this review may contain spoilers---

A few (subjective) criticisms:
Some of the abilities put you in a very long animation that leave you very susceptible to instantly dying or losing almost all of your health and as a result, there are 3 abilities I rarely use. [b]edit: Some abilities now have a short period of invincibility after activation.[/b]
QTEs are unnecessary.
There is some amount of sway on the sniper while moving which I personally do not like, but I understand if it's necessary in order balance the weapons.
Since the game is so short, upgrades do not feel extremely significant, but they still add a lot of damage and are useful. I'm unsure how to word my feelings on this.
The sneaking sequence is a bit annoying. Killing someone from behind sticks you in a long kill animation. Killing someone from the front is instantaneous. This means killing someone from the front and narrowly avoiding maxing the detection bar is safe but if you kill someone from behind and an enemy walks close to you during this long animation, you are guaranteed to die unless there nearby cover, which quite possibly wont help at all as all enemies have been alerted. It IS possible to clear the entire area after having alerted the guards, but that doesn't excuse the issue.
It wasn't obvious to me that I was invisible in the grasses because of how easy it was to see through them, but I did figure it out quickly. I assume this is a necessary evil due to camera position.
The weapon secondaries, although they are all unique, feel like they should be saved to kill bosses faster, which puts them in a weird place. The sheer damage benefit from nuking boss hp with the secondaries feels like too much to give up for destroying normal enemies with ease.
While abilities work well on just two buttons and there was clearly thought put into how to make that work, I would prefer if they were split across more buttons.

Objective criticisms:
It's too short.
For stealth areas, there is a sound alert when you are close to being detected, but it is delayed and it does not cancel if the bar is nearly empty--I had many situations where I was almost detected, killed an enemy, and when my bar was more than half empty, I got the loud warning noise. Currently, the warning noise is kind of useless.

Random notes:
The game gives you enough tools to play extremely aggressively without ever retreating even once, but also allows you to play safely from a distance or even mix the two.
There is a good variation of dodging vs blocking. Small learning curve, good gameplay variation, feels good. I still need to mess around and see if how much I can use aerial gameplay to dodge, as that would likely be quite fun.

In terms of graphics and gameplay, it was very beautiful and enjoyable. However, I did not know what was going on in the story.

If Bright Memory were a hand grenade, Bright Memory: Infinite would be a Hydrogen Bomb. 

Everything is improved at dramatic levels, the good shooting is now excellent, the decent hack 'n' slash is now fantastic, and the great graphics are now gorgeous. 

The story and universe are still a mess, but now there is a bit of development here and there. Still just an excuse to shoot stuff.

The gameplay has been upgraded A LOT. Now we have more weapons, and the weapons have secondary fire modes that can also be upgraded. A lot more skills and upgrades were added, and the sword became a murder machine.

As for the levels, it's a mix of Chinese villages and temples, all being sucked out by a black hole. It's always raining and windy, so the scenario's foliage is a joy to look at. I read somewhere that some scenarios and props were scanned and inserted in the game, like Ninja Theory with Hellblade, the results are phenomenal.

As for the performance, yeah, not as good as the original. Naturally, the game is much more complex, so it requires much more firepower, however my gripes are regarding UE/DX12 shader stutters and not frames. After a while, it maintained a steady framerate even with Ray Tracing on and Native 1440p. I booted in DX11 once by accident, and it was running over 240FPS, but I had already played quite a bit. Maybe compiling shaders before playing? Who knows.

My Bright Memory: Infinite run clocked in at 2 hours, and besides the bad story, the only critique I have is that I wish it was longer. It's a superb game, and it's even more absurd that it was mostly made by one dev.

Let me start off by saying I was enjoying this at first. The combat is fun and chaining combos together doesn't get old. I was about an hour deep and thinking I'd probably recommend this despite some flaws due to the reasonably low price. I started to think about how to word that and make it clear that this is a budget shooter and don't expect much beyond that.

But then the paint chips away and the problems start adding up and I'm sitting here wondering why am I trying to make excuses for what is a flawed game? There's at least two massive problems that I just can't forgive:

1. I keep getting stuck in terrain, which requires restarting from a checkpoint. (and when I'm not getting stuck in terrain, the enemies are which detracts from the combat fun) the world is just janky with too many invisible walls and and poor AI pathing. I don't think this can be fixed without a redesign.

2. It crashes frequently, this may get fixed some day, though it is built in UE4, which is crash prone for some people no matter what.
---

With that noted let me continue more in the direction I was originally going before being stuck and it's this:

Judged purely as a low budget shooter, it's fun with interesting combos and powerups and if that's all you want from a game you wouldn't need me to say anything else about it.

However, that still comes with some pretty big notes, if you're expecting anything beyond that:

1. Level design is linear corridors, you have enough space to slide around for dodges but there's no exploration or strategic options to approach combat.

2. Enemies are bullet sponges, the bosses are bigger bullet sponges that sometimes refill their health bar after you kill them so you get to kill them twice, because what's more fun than a big bullet sponge than a big bullet sponge with double the health? It can be kind of immersion breaking to be given a sniper rifle and then still need to shoot someone 10 times in the head before he dies.

3. The story is childish nonsense. The kind of nonsense where a black hole can be sitting in the sky above you and it's strong enough to suck in airplanes from the other side of the world, but you and the things closer to it are just fine, because, plot armor. I won't harp too much on the dumb story, this is just a budget shooter, I'm just saying don't expect any of it to make sense outside of "we did this cuz a 5 year old would think it's cool"

4. The game is somewhat short, depending on your skill level it's maybe 60 to 90 minutes of actual play area. If you get stuck repeating areas it will obviously take longer, but that's not "more content" that's you repeating the same. Likewise the higher difficulty options may take longer simply because: if it took you 5 minutes of shooting the boss in the head on normal it's going to take you 10 minutes on hard to dump extra bullets into the sponge.

5. The combat system has a lot of depth and variety, but it takes a lot of powerups to complete all the systems, but the game is so short you barely get to use them all. In fact you usually learn how to do something (like wall jumping) use it once or twice and then not really see it again. It's almost like the entire game is one long tutorial and once you've learned how to use everything, it's just over.

6. The forced stealth sections are so poorly designed they shouldn't even be in the game.  They are so bad in so many ways that I could honestly write an entire review just on how bad the stealth sections are. I'll give one example to keep this brief: Stealth up behind two guards and start the stealth-kill on one of them, control is taken from you while the game animates the stealth-kill. There's your character hacking away at the guards legs, then his arms, then his back, then his head, all the while he's screaming in pain from all this hacking and slashing and the guard next to him hears nothing because, stealth kill, you attacked from behind. Why didn't the character just silently cut the guards throat across his unprotected neck? I mean, it still would be dumb that the other guard didn't hear the body fall but at least there wouldn't be screaming that's being ignored. There's so many other things wrong with the stealth sections…

7. I don't feel compelled to replay and there's no extra content. Not that I expect a ton of extra content in a $20 game, but there's just the one short campaign, the story is nonsense and the only reason to play again is to prove you can beat it on a higher difficulty with enemies that are even bigger bullet sponges. You'll be doing the same dodge/attacks at every difficulty level, it's just a question of whether the enemy takes 5 of them to kill or 500. 

8. The combat system, while fun, doesn't actually make a lot of sense. Your character just has magical powers because it seems like a fun idea, but there's no real attempt at explaining it and what little is mentioned is convoluted at best. Since when does an EMP cause someone to float in the air and then be able to toss them around? That's not an electromagnetic pulse, that's just telekinetics. And that type of zero-logic is pervasive throughout. You have a sword that can block almost anything and deflect bullets. But you're human? And don't tell me "it's the exo-suit doing it" because if that's the case: why am I the one activating the block? Shouldn't the suit just block for you on its own? You're a human that is literally faster than a bullet, not because it makes sense or gets explained in any way, but just because, it's fun.

9. The game progression makes very little sense. You're handed a new gun pretty much every chapter, it's not always an upgrade to what you have, like you are given a pistol after you already have an assault rifle and a shotgun and there's literally no valid purpose to the pistol other than to bloat the number of weapons in the game. Or the amount of alternate ammo types, I think there's more ammo types than there are enemy types. I never even found a use for most of the weapons or alt-ammo. And the game is built in a way that you can finish it without needing any particular upgrades, so you can build your powerups any way you want, but they never feel needed.

I could list more issues, but those are the basics.

Things I could praise it for:

1. Voice acting adequate for a budget title. The story may be pointless but at least you won't be sick of listening to it immediately.

2. The music is decent.

3. It's visually interesting. It's no better than any other Unreal 4 Engine game in quality, but it's got some fun enemy designs and despite being a small world it was enjoyable to look at.

4. The real stand out and primary selling point is the combat system. If you just overlook the poor story telling elements surrounding it and just accept it as game play, well, you can have a lot of fun just tossing enemies around, slashing them up or shooting them with a variety of guns that you mostly don't need (since your sword is typically stronger and you start with it)
